explain.say: Every few minutes, grid control rooms from India to Brazil run a calculation called load flow, to check that no line is overloaded and every voltage is healthy. On the board is a tiny grid: two generators and a city using 200 megawatts, joined by three identical lines, each 0.1 per unit. How does the power choose its path?

explain.say: First, each bus, or node, gets a type. Load buses are PQ: we know the real and reactive power they draw. Generator buses are PV: we set their output and voltage. And one generator is the slack bus: it covers whatever is left over, including losses, and its angle is the zero reference. Why do we need one bus that is left free?

groups.ask: What are slack, PV and PQ buses?

draw.text: Slack: V, δ fixed | PV: P, V fixed | PQ: P, Q fixed

explain.say: Because nobody knows the losses until the answer is found. Now the physics. Real power flows from a higher voltage angle to a lower one, roughly the angle difference divided by the line reactance. Solving our grid gives the city bus about minus 6.7 degrees and bus 2 about minus 1.9. So 116.7 megawatts go straight from bus 1, and 83.3 from bus 2. Why does bus 1 also feed bus 2?

explain.say: Because power takes every path, shared in inverse proportion to impedance. The route from bus 1 through bus 2 is twice as long as the direct line, so it carries less, but not zero. Check the balance: bus 2 receives 33.3, makes 50, and sends 83.3 to the city. Power in equals power out at every bus. What would happen if the direct line tripped?

explain.say: All 200 megawatts would squeeze through bus 2's line, which might overload: exactly what load flow studies check. Real grids have thousands of buses, and the full AC equations are non-linear, so computers use Newton–Raphson: guess, find the mismatch, correct, repeat. Superb! Exam tip: the slack bus balances the losses.

faq.a: It calculates the voltage magnitude and angle at every bus of a power network, and from them the real and reactive power in every line, for a given pattern of generation and load. Operators use it to check for overloads and low voltages.
asks: What is a power flow study?

faq.q: What are slack, PV and PQ buses?
faq.a: A PQ bus is a load with known real and reactive power. A PV bus is a generator with known real power and voltage. The slack bus is one generator whose voltage and angle are fixed; it supplies whatever power balances the system, including losses.

faq.q: How does power split between parallel paths?
faq.a: Power divides among all available paths in inverse proportion to their reactance. A direct line of 0.1 per unit carries twice the share of a two-line route totalling 0.2 per unit.
asks: Why does power take more than one path?

faq.q: What is the DC load flow approximation?
faq.a: It assumes flat voltages, no resistance and small angles, so the real power on a line is simply the angle difference divided by its reactance. That makes load flow a set of fast linear equations, good for quick planning studies.

faq.q: Why is Newton-Raphson used for load flow?
faq.a: The AC power flow equations are non-linear. Newton-Raphson linearises them with a Jacobian matrix, corrects the guess and repeats, usually converging in a handful of iterations even for thousands of buses.

facts: The July 2012 blackouts in northern India affected more than 600 million people.
In DC load flow, real power on a line is approximately (δi − δj)/X in per unit.
Newton–Raphson load flow typically converges in about 3 to 5 iterations.

quiz.say: A line has a reactance of 0.1 per unit and an angle difference of 0.05 radians. Using DC load flow on a 100 megavolt-ampere base, what power flows?
quiz.show: A line has X = 0.1 pu and an angle difference of 0.05 rad. Using DC load flow on a 100 MVA base, what power flows?
quiz.why: P equals 0.05 over 0.1, which is 0.5 per unit, times 100 megavolt-amperes: 50 megawatts.

wrong.1: That multiplies 0.05 by 0.1 instead of dividing.
wrong.2: That divides 0.1 by 0.05, the wrong way round.
